title: Test what you staged, not what is on disk
summary: You staged a subset of your changes for a clean commit. Before committing, run the tests against exactly that subset — with stash --keep-index — and stash only selected hunks.
concepts: verifying a commit before making it
mental_model: `--keep-index` stashes everything but leaves the index applied to your working tree. What is on disk then equals exactly what your next commit will contain — so a test run is a test of the commit, not of your desk.

write.content:
from dosing import dose


def check():
    assert dose(2) == 2.7
    return 'ok'


print(check())
print('SCRATCH DEBUGGING — must not be committed')

from dosing import dose


def check():
    assert dose(2) == 2.7
    return 'ok'


print(check())
print('local scratch assertion')

steps.title: Stage the part you intend to ship
steps.why: The validation fix belongs in the commit. The debug file and the scratch line in the test do not. Staging is easy — the hard part is being sure the staged set actually works on its own.
steps.expect: dosing.py staged; test_dosing.py modified and debug.py untracked, both unstaged.

steps.title: The trap: running tests proves nothing
steps.why: Running anything now tests your working tree, which contains scratch edits that are not going into the commit. Plenty of broken commits pass local tests for exactly this reason.
steps.expect: The scratch line and debug.py are present — they would be part of any test run.

steps.title: Stash everything except the index
steps.why: `--keep-index` parks the unstaged and untracked changes, then restores the staged state onto your working tree. Disk now equals the future commit exactly.
commands: git stash push -u --keep-index -m "scratch: debug and local test line"
steps.expect: debug.py gone, test file back to its committed version, dosing.py still holding the staged fix.

verify.label: …while the staged change stays on disk
the debug file is parked too

steps.title: Now the test run means something
steps.why: What you run here is precisely what CI will run after your commit lands. This one habit catches the entire class of 'works on my machine' commits.
steps.expect: Only the intended change, nothing else in sight.

steps.title: Commit with confidence, then restore your desk
steps.why: Commit the verified set, then pop the stash to get your scratch work back. Two commands, and the commit is provably self-contained.
steps.expect: The commit contains one file; your debug file and scratch line come back.

verify.label: and your scratch work is back

steps.title: Stash only some paths
steps.why: `git stash push -- <path>` parks specific files and leaves the rest alone. Simpler than hunks when the split happens to fall on file boundaries.
commands: git stash push -u -m "just the debug file" -- debug.py
steps.expect: debug.py parked; the test file's scratch line still in the working tree.

verify.label: …and the other change was left alone

steps.title: Clean up
steps.why: `git stash clear` deletes every entry. It is the one stash command with no undo, so read `git stash list` before running it.

verify.label: the commit contains the validation fix
verify.hint: stage dosing.py, stash the rest with --keep-index, then commit

verify.label: …and nothing else — no scratch file, no scratch test line
the committed code is the validated version

pitfalls: `--keep-index` without `-u` leaves untracked files in place, which defeats the purpose — a stray new module still pollutes the test run.
If the tests fail during a `--keep-index` run, the fix is to amend the index and try again. Do not pop first, or you lose the isolation.
`git stash push -p` walks hunks interactively, the same picker as `git add -p`.
`git stash --staged` (git 2.35+) does the inverse: it stashes the staged changes and leaves your working tree alone.
cheatsheet: park everything but leave the staged state on disk
park what is staged, keep the rest
confirm what the commit will contain
